title: What did it cost?
html:
It seems great to be smart, jacked, and wealthy, but people seldom consider the cost of achieving such things.

For example, people like to idolize entrepreneurs.

“I wish I could be like them,” you think.

But what if you were?

Congratulations! You’re Elon Musk. Now what?

Your hands tremble with joy as you check the balance of your bank account. You laugh at all the commas.

But before you get a chance to scroll through your contact list filled with celebrities, your phone rings.

And then it rings again.

And then again.

Your companies are on fire—all of them—and if you don’t act fast, the fires will spread.

With your heart racing and sweat dripping down your face, you make your way to the Gigafactory and get to work.

You won’t get to spend time with your kids tonight

…or enjoy a meal with your friends

…or put an ounce of thought into the shitpost you’re about make on X.

You won’t get to enjoy many of the things that seem to make life worth living.

Why?

Because you’re an entrepreneur.

Now, bring to mind your current circumstances.

Consider all the beautiful things in your life. I’d bet my almost-non-existent graduate student salary on the idea that, if you chose the path of the entrepreneur (assuming you’re not already on it), many of those things would vanish.

Everything has a cost, and the price of being exceptional is that you must forgo things that non-exceptional people cherish. But please note that I’m not making any moral judgment against non-exceptionalism. People have every right to follow the herd: to party; to eat fast food; to work a cushy 9-to-5. Fundamentally, I believe people should do what fulfills them. And if Tito’s, KFC, and a 9-to-5 really do it for you, fine! Then you’ll just be average, and that’s okay.

But if you want to be anything other than average, if you want to be exceptional, you must be prepared to sacrifice average in exchange for excellence. And the amount of excellence you achieve will be proportional to the amount of sacrifice you make to achieve it.

So, perhaps it’d be best to think twice about who we envy. We might not want to front the cost of being them.
